reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Most common congenital disorder of glycosylation; a multisystem N-glycosylation defect caused by biallelic PMM2 variants
Classic infantile presentation combines failure to thrive, developmental delay, hypotonia and a cerebellar/pontocerebellar hypoplasia picture
Distinctive dysmorphic clues include inverted nipples and abnormal (fat pad) subcutaneous fat distribution over the buttocks and suprapubic area
Non-neurological features include pericardial effusion, hepatopathy, coagulopathy, hypothyroidism and stroke-like episodes
Older children develop retinitis pigmentosa, peripheral neuropathy, ataxia, skeletal changes and hypogonadism
Screening test is serum transferrin isoform analysis showing a type 1 pattern (raised asialo- and disialotransferrin) reflecting whole-glycan loss
Enzyme assay of phosphomannomutase in leukocytes/fibroblasts and PMM2 gene sequencing confirm the diagnosis
Management is supportive and multidisciplinary; there is no disease-modifying therapy, though dietary mannose supplementation has been tried without proven benefit
reference.pathophysiology: PMM2-CDG results from deficiency of phosphomannomutase 2, the cytosolic enzyme that converts mannose-6-phosphate to mannose-1-phosphate, an essential step in generating GDP-mannose and the dolichol-linked oligosaccharide precursor used for N-linked glycosylation of proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum. Reduced substrate limits assembly and transfer of the glycan, so many secretory and membrane glycoproteins are hypoglycosylated, with whole glycan chains missing from some sialylation sites. Because glycosylation is required across virtually every organ system, the resulting glycoprotein dysfunction produces the characteristic multisystem phenotype affecting the brain and cerebellum, liver, heart, endocrine glands, coagulation factors and connective tissue. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
additionalDifferentials: Other congenital disorders of glycosylation (e.g. ALG6-CDG, MPI-CDG)
Congenital muscular dystrophies with cerebellar involvement
Peroxisomal disorders such as Zellweger spectrum
Pontocerebellar hypoplasia of other genetic cause
Inherited coagulopathies presenting with unexplained bleeding/thrombosis
additionalInvestigations: Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry (type 1 pattern)
Phosphomannomutase enzyme activity in leukocytes or fibroblasts
PMM2 gene sequencing for confirmation and family counselling
Coagulation studies including antithrombin, protein C, protein S and factor XI
Thyroid function tests and liver function/transaminases
Brain MRI to demonstrate cerebellar/pontocerebellar hypoplasia
Echocardiography for pericardial effusion and cardiomyopathy
redFlags: Stroke-like episodes or thrombotic events reflecting coagulation factor imbalance
Life-threatening pericardial effusion or cardiac failure in infancy
Severe hepatopathy with hypoalbuminaemia and protein-losing enteropathy
Acute deterioration during intercurrent illness with multi-organ failure
Progressive feeding failure and profound failure to thrive
reference.prognosis: Infantile mortality can reach up to one in five, often from infection, cardiac or hepatic complications; survivors have static intellectual disability with slowly progressive neurological and multisystem involvement, and prognosis varies widely with genotype and severity.
pitfalls: Attributing the picture to a non-specific 'cerebral palsy' and never testing transferrin glycoforms
False-negative or false-positive transferrin patterns in neonates, intercurrent infection, galactosaemia or heavy alcohol exposure
Overlooking treatable comorbidities such as hypothyroidism and coagulopathy before procedures
Assuming mannose supplementation is effective, unlike its role in MPI-CDG
Not screening for thrombosis/bleeding risk prior to surgery or anticoagulation decisions
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease (OMMBID)
Jaeken J, Inborn Errors of Metabolism: Diagnosis and Treatment
management: No curative therapy exists; care is multisystem supportive management coordinated by metabolic medicine
Nutritional support for failure to thrive, including enteral tube feeding where oral intake is inadequate
Correct and monitor the coagulopathy (antithrombin, protein C and S, factor XI), with clotting-factor replacement around surgery or bleeding
Thyroid hormone replacement for hypothyroidism, with ongoing endocrine surveillance
Monitor and manage hepatopathy, pericardial effusion and cardiac involvement
Developmental support, physiotherapy for hypotonia and ataxia, and ophthalmology review for retinitis pigmentosa
Anticipate and treat stroke-like episodes and thrombotic events, avoiding dehydration and other provoking factors
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder, with carrier testing and prenatal counselling for the family
